title: Theorem
body_md:
{[Vague form]}
Suppose that $\mathbb{K}$ is an ATR field of degree $n = r+2 \geq 3$. Fix an integral ideal $\mathfrak{f} \neq \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$. Fix an integral ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ of norm $N$ coprime to $q$ such that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/\mathfrak{a}$ is cyclic. Fix an integral ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$. Fix a set of fundamental units $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$ for some group of totally positive units in $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ and consider the cycle $\Upsilon$ attached to these units. Under mild assumptions on $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}$ and $\Upsilon$, there is a compatible set of admissible base points $(h_{\rho})_{\rho}$ for the data $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \Upsilon$. Moreover, the size of the product (\ref{uvagueformun}) associated to this choice of base points is bounded by quantities depending only on $\mathfrak{f}$ and $\Upsilon$.

label: defsmoothingideal
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defsmoothingideal}
An integral ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ is a smoothing ideal for $\mathfrak{f}$ (resp. for $\mathfrak{f}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$) if the quotient $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/\mathfrak{a}$ is a cyclic abelian group of order $N$ such that $N$ is coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$ (resp. $N$ is coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$ and to $\mathfrak{b}$). The integer $N$ is then called the smoothing index.
head: environment

label: defadmissible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defadmissible}
A base point $h \in L = \mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ is admissible (for the data $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}$) if $h/q \equiv 1 \mathrm{~mod~} L$ and $h/N$ generates the cyclic group $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L/L \simeq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$. A base point $h \in L$ is simply called ``weakly admissible'' if $h/q \equiv k\cdot \varepsilon \mathrm{~mod~} L$ for some $k \in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and $\varepsilon \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}$ and $h/N$ generates the cyclic group $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L/L \simeq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$

label: defcompatible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defcompatible}
The family of admissible base points $(h_{\rho})_{\rho}$ is compatible (for the data $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$) if and only if the ideal $\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L)$ is independent of $\rho$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider two such admissible base points $h, h' \in \mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$. Since $(h/m)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} = (h'/m')\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$, there is a unit $\xi \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}^{\times}$ such that $h/m = \xi h'/m'$. Then, we have:
$$\mathrm{det}_{B_L}(h', u_1h', \dots, u_rh', y) = \mathcal{N}(\xi) \left(\frac{m}{m'}\right)^{r+1} \mathrm{det}_{B_L}(h, u_1 h, \dots, u_rh, \xi^{-1}y).$$
Hence $\lambda = \lambda'$ and $a'= \mathcal{N}(\xi) \cdot a(\xi^{-1}\cdot)$ where $\mathcal{N}(\xi) = \pm 1$. For any $x, y \in \mathbb{K}$, the conditions $a(xy) \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $a(\xi^{-1}xy) \in \mathbb{Z}$ are equivalent, therefore, by definition of $\mathfrak{D}(a, L)$ and $\mathfrak{D}(a', L)$ we get $\mathfrak{D}(a, L) = \mathfrak{D}(a', L)$.

label: conjecture
title: Main Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conjecture}
Suppose that $\mathbb{K}$ is an ATR field of degree $n = r+2 \geq 3$. Fix an integral ideal $\mathfrak{f} \neq \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$. Set $q\mathbb{Z} = \mathfrak{f} \cap \mathbb{Z}$ with $q >0$. Let $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ be one of the two complex embeddings of $\mathbb{K}$ and fix a complex embedding $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f})$ which extends $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$. Fix a smoothing ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ of norm $N$ coprime to $q$. Fix a class $\mathfrak{c}$ in the narrow ray class group at $\mathfrak{f}$. Fix an integer $\kappa > 0$ coprime to $q$ and an integral ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$ such that the integral ideal $\kappa\cdot\mathfrak{b}$ belongs to the class $\mathfrak{c}$. Fix a set of non-degenerate fundamental units $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$ for $U_{\mathfrak{f}}^+$. Assume that there exists a compatible set of admissible base points $\underline{h}$ for the data $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is an orientation datum $(\mu_{\rho}, \nu_{\rho}, k_{\rho}, \varepsilon_{\rho})_{\rho}$ depending on $\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r, (h_{\rho})_{\rho}$ for which the following Kronecker limit formula holds:
\begin{equation}\label{klfconjecture}
N\zeta'_{\mathfrak{f}}(\mathfrak{c}, 0) - \zeta'_{\mathfrak{f}}(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{c}, 0) = \log\left|I_{r,\mathfrak{f}, \kappa\cdot\mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r ; \underline{h}, \underline{\mu}, \underline{\nu}, (k_{\rho}, \varepsilon_{\rho})_{\rho})\right|^2.
\end{equation}
Any such orientation datum shall be called ``correct'' (for the data $\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r, \underline{h}$).
\item For the fixed data $\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r, \underline{h}$, the complex number
$$\mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r, \underline{h}) = I_{r,\mathfrak{f}, \kappa\cdot\mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r ; \underline{h}, \underline{\mu}, \underline{\nu}, (k_{\rho}, \varepsilon_{\rho})_{\rho})^{\mathcal{D}(N, n)} $$
is independent of the choice of correct orientation datum.
\item For the fixed data $\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}, \varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$, the complex number 
$$\mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r) = \mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r, \underline{h})$$
is independent of the choice of compatible set of admissible base points $\underline{h}$.
\item For the fixed data $\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}$, the complex number 
$$\mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}= \mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r)$$
is independent of the choice of non-degenerate fundamental units $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$ for $U_{\mathfrak{f}}^+$ (for which there exists at least one compatible set of base points $\underline{h}$).
\item For the fixed data $\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}$, the complex number 
$$\mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}}= \mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}$$
is independent of the choice of representation of the class $\mathfrak{c}$ by the pair $\kappa, \mathfrak{b}$ such that the integral ideal $\kappa \cdot \mathfrak{b}$ belongs to the class $\mathfrak{c}$.
\item The complex number $\mathcal{V}_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}}$ is the image in $\mathbb{C}$ of an algebraic unit $u_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}}$ in the class field $\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f})$ under the complex embedding $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f})$.
\item Any embedding of $\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f})$ above a real embedding of $\mathbb{K}$ maps $u_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}}$ to the unit circle.
\item If $\mathfrak{c}'$ is a class in the narrow ray class group at $\mathfrak{f}$ then the explicit reciprocity law is given by
$$\sigma_{\mathfrak{c}'}(u_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{a}}) = u_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{c}\mathfrak{c}', \mathfrak{a}} $$
where $\mathfrak{c} \to \sigma_{\mathfrak{c}}$ is the Artin map.
\item For a fixed integral ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$, the algebraic units $u_{\mathfrak{f}, \kappa \cdot \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}$ obtained when varying $\kappa \in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}/\mathcal{Z}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{1, +}$ are conjugated in the field extension $\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f})/\mathbb{K}^{+}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Remarks
body_md:
\begin{enumerate} 
\item In the case $n = 2$, that is for imaginary quadratic fields, it is already known (see section \ref{reviewquadratic}) that the values 
$$\theta_{\mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{a}}^{\pm}(h)^{\mathcal{D}(N, 2)}$$
are $q$-units in abelian extensions of imaginary quadratic fields as a consequence of the theory of Complex Multiplication and that they satisfy the second limit formula due to Kronecker.
\item In the case $n = 3$, the Kronecker limit formula is already proven in \cite{BCG} and the invariance statements 2-5 hold for the absolute values of these complex numbers as a consequence. The invariance statements 2-4 have been proven very recently in \cite{TeymourGray} under mild hypotheses on $N$ (that is for the complex numbers themselves and not only for their absolute values). The statements regarding the algebraic nature of these complex numbers remain conjectural.
\item Correct orientations in the conjecture may be computed by checking which ones among the $(2\cdot 2 \cdot \#\mathcal{Z}_{\mathfrak{f}}^1/\mathcal{Z}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{1, +})^{r!}$ possible choices give the desired Kronecker limit formula (\ref{klfconjecture}). For the most simple examples, the quotient $\mathcal{Z}_{\mathfrak{f}}^1/\langle \mathcal{Z}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{1, +}, (q-1, -1)\rangle$ is trivial and we only need to compute the orientation signs $\mu_{\rho}, \nu_{\rho}$. In many cases, the orientations may be taken as:
$$\mu_{\rho} = \nu_{\rho} = \mathrm{sgn}(\rho) \cdot \mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{Reg}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r)) $$
where $\mathrm{sign}(\mathrm{Reg}(\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r))$ is the sign of the regulator of $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_r$ computing with this order on fundamental units, and the fixed order on the embeddings of $\mathbb{K}$. These orientations are inspired by orientation conditions described in the study of (signed) Shintani fundamental domains in \cite{Colmez}, \cite{Diazydiaz} and \cite{Espinoza}. Exploring possible connections between our geometric constructions and Espinoza's signed fundamental domains for ATR fields might give us an explicit description of correct orientation data in our conjecture.

label: tmin

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Consider the matrices $U,V \in \mathrm{GL}_{r+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $U\mathcal{A}V = S(\mathcal{A})$ is the Smith normal form of $\mathcal{A}$. Then
$$ dI_{r+1} = U (dI_{r+1})U^{-1}= U \mathcal{A} \mathcal{B}' U^{-1} =\left(U \mathcal{A} V\right) \cdot \left(V^{-1} \mathcal{B}' U^{-1}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} t & 0 & \dots & 0 \\ 0 & A_{r-1} & \dots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & \dots & \dots & 1  \end{pmatrix} V^{-1} \mathcal{B}' U^{-1}.$$
Since $V^{-1} \mathcal{B}' U^{-1} \in M_{r+1}(\mathbb{Z})$, the first row of $S(\mathcal{A})\times V^{-1} \mathcal{B}' U^{-1}$ is divisible by $t$ and therefore $t$ divides $d$. \smallskip

(ii) Let $\underline{\alpha}' = (\alpha'_0, \dots, \alpha'_r)$ be a uniform positive dual family to $\underline{a}$ in $L$ such that $\underline{a} \cdot \underline{\alpha}' = dI_{r+1}$. Write the coordinates of the $\alpha'_j$ in the basis $B_L$ as $\alpha'_j = \sum_{i = 0}^{r+1} b'_{ij} e_i$. Then the matrix $\mathcal{B}' = (b_{ij}')_{1 \leq i,j \leq r+1}$ satisfies $\mathcal{A} \cdot \mathcal{B}' = d I_{r+1}$ and thus, by (i), $t$ divides $d$. \smallskip

(iii) Suppose that $\underline{a} \cdot \underline{\alpha} = dI_{r+1}$ and $\underline{a} \cdot \underline{\alpha}' = d' I_{r+1}$. Write as before the coordinates of $\alpha_0, \dots, \alpha_r$ and $\alpha'_0, \dots, \alpha'_r$ as:
$$\alpha_j = \sum_{i = 0}^{r+1} b_{ij} e_i ~~ \text{ and } ~~  \alpha'_j = \sum_{i = 0}^{r+1} b'_{ij} e_i.$$
Then the matrices $\mathcal{B} = (b_{ij})_{1 \leq i,j \leq r+1} \in M_{r+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathcal{B}' = (b'_{ij})_{1 \leq i,j \leq r+1} \in M_{r+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ satisfy $\mathcal{A}\mathcal{B} =dI_{r+1}$ and $\mathcal{A} \mathcal{B}' = d' I_{r+1}$. Since $\mathcal{A}$ is invertible, it follows that $d'\mathcal{B} = d\mathcal{B}'$. Thus, for any $0 \leq j \leq r$: 
$$d'\alpha_j - d\alpha'_j = (d'b_{0j}-db'_{0j})e_0 =  (d'b_{0j}-db'_{0j})\eta \gamma \in \mathrm{gcd}(d, d')\mathbb{Z} \gamma$$ 
as claimed.

label: tahpdf
title: Proof
body_md:
We shall prove simultaneously the three points of this proposition. We use formula (\ref{eqlienata}) which relates the linear forms $a$ and $\tilde{a}$ in conjunction with (\ref{defa}) and (\ref{eqdeftf}) to evaluate $\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h)$ for any $0 \leq j, k \leq r$. Indeed:
$$\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) = \mathrm{det}_{B_L}(h, u_1 h, \dots, u_r h, u_k\tilde{\alpha}_j h).$$
Using standard linear algebra and the definition of the norm of the fractional ideal $L$ we may rewrite this equality using $\mathrm{det}_{\tilde{B}}$  instead of $\mathrm{det}_{B_L}$ as
\begin{align*}
\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) & = \mathrm{det}_{B_L}(\tilde{B}) \mathrm{det}_{\tilde{B}}(h, u_1h, \dots, u_rh, u_k \tilde{\alpha}_jh)\\
\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) &=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}(L)}\mathrm{det}_{\tilde{B}}(h, u_1h, \dots, u_rh, u_k \tilde{\alpha}_jh).
\end{align*}
Then, using the definition of the norm $\mathcal{N}(h)$ of $h$ we get
\begin{align*}
\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) & = \frac{\mathcal{N}(h)}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \mathrm{det}_{\tilde{B}}(1, u_1, \dots, u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j)\\
\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) & = \frac{\mathcal{N}(h)}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \tilde{\lambda} \tilde{a} (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j).
\end{align*}
We now use formula (\ref{deftalpha}) to conclude that for $k \neq j$, $a (u_k \tilde{\alpha}_j h) = 0$ and for $k = j$: 
$$\lambda m^{r+1} a (u_j \tilde{\alpha}_j h) = \frac{\mathcal{N}(h)}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \tilde{\lambda} \tilde{t}$$
which we may rewrite as:
\begin{equation}\label{tahpdf}
a u_j \tilde{\alpha}_j h = \frac{\mathcal{N}(h)}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lambda m^{r+1}} \tilde{t} \neq 0.
\end{equation}
The lattice $L$ is a fractional ideal and $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$, therefore $\tilde{\alpha}_0h, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r h \in L$ and since $a \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(L, \mathbb{Z})$, the rational number 
$$ d = \frac{\mathcal{N}(h)}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lambda m^{r+1}} \tilde{t}$$
is actually a non-zero integer whose sign is $\epsilon = \epsilon_h = \mathrm{sign}(\mathcal{N}(h))$. We have proven that $\epsilon \tilde{\underline{\alpha}} h$ is a uniform positive dual family to $\underline{a}$ in $L$ such that 
$$\underline{a} \cdot (\epsilon \tilde{\underline{\alpha}} h) = \epsilon d I_{r+1} = |d| I_{r+1}.$$
Let us now rewrite this using the level $\ell$ (see Definition \ref{definitionlevel}). By definition, there are integers $m_0, \dots, m_r$ and elements $\beta_0, \dots, \beta_r \in L$ such that for any $0 \leq j \leq r$:
$$\tilde{\alpha}_jh = \epsilon (\ell m \beta_j - m_j h).$$
Then (\ref{tahpdf}) may be written in terms of $\beta_j$ as:
$$a(u_k \beta_j) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ if } j \neq k \\ \frac{|d|}{m\ell} = \frac{|\mathcal{N}(h/m)|}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lambda} \frac{\tilde{t}}{\ell} & \text{ if } j = k.\end{cases} $$
The elements $u_k\beta_j$ belong to $L$ therefore $a(u_k\beta_j) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for any $0 \leq j,k \leq r$ and $\beta_0, \dots, \beta_r$ is a uniform positive dual family to $a, au_1, \dots, au_r$ in $L$. It follows from lemma \ref{tmin} that $t$ divides the integer $d/(m\ell)$. We now prove that $t m \ell = |d|$. Indeed, it follows from lemma \ref{tmin}, (iii) that for any $0 \leq j \leq r$:
$$\frac{|d|}{m\ell} \alpha_j - t \beta_j \in t\mathbb{Z} \gamma.$$ 
Replacing $\beta_j$ by its definition we obtain:
$$\frac{d}{m\ell t} \alpha_j -   \frac{(\tilde{\alpha}_j +m_j)h}{m \ell} \in \mathbb{Z} \gamma$$
and thus:
$$ \tilde{\alpha}_jh \in \frac{d}{t} \alpha_j -m_jh +m\ell \mathbb{Z}\gamma$$ 
This shows in particular that 
$$\tilde{\alpha}_0h, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_rh \in \frac{|d|}{t} L + \mathbb{Z} \gamma $$
and therefore the inequality $|d|/t \leq m \ell$ holds. This may be written as $|d| \leq m\ell t$ and the fact that $m \ell t$ divides $|d|$ with $|d| > 0$ implies that $|d| \geq m \ell t$. Thus the two quantities must be equal. We have thus proven that $\underline{a} \cdot (\epsilon \tilde{\underline{\alpha}} h) = |d| I_{r+1} = m \ell t I_{r+1}$ and that the fundamental equality:
$$ \lambda \ell t = \frac{|\mathcal{N}(h/m)|}{\mathcal{N}(L)} \tilde{\lambda} \tilde{t}$$
holds in $\mathbb{Z}$. The identification of $\beta_j$ with $\alpha_j$ gives the desired relation between the families $\underline{\alpha}$, $\tilde{\underline{\alpha}}$:
$$\alpha_j = \frac{\tilde{\alpha}_j h + m_j h}{\epsilon m \ell}. $$

label: definitiondifferent
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{definitiondifferent}
Let $f : \mathbb{K} \to \mathbb{Q}$ be a non-zero $\mathbb{Q}$-linear form on $\mathbb{K}$. Let $I$ be a fractional ideal of $\mathbb{K}$. The fractional ideal $\mathfrak{D}(f, I)$ defined by:
$$\mathfrak{D}(f, I)^{-1} = \{ x \in \mathbb{K} ~|~ \forall\, y \in I, f(xy) \in \mathbb{Z}\}$$
is called the different ideal of $f$ on $I$ by analogy with the usual different ideal $\mathfrak{d}$ of $\mathbb{K}$ given by $\mathfrak{d} = \mathfrak{D}(\operatorname{Tr}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}})$.
head: environment

label: lemmabasicdifferent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmabasicdifferent}
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If $I' = \beta I$ for some $\beta \in \mathbb{K}^{\times}$ then $\mathfrak{D}(f, I') = \beta \cdot \mathfrak{D}(f, I)$.
\item[(ii)] If $I = I_1 + I_2$ then $\mathfrak{D}(f, I) = \mathfrak{D}(f, I_1) + \mathfrak{D}(f, I_2)$.
\item[(iii)] For any fractional ideal $I$ of $\mathbb{K}$, $\mathfrak{D}(f, I) = I \cdot \mathfrak{D}(f, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}})$.
\item[(iv)] If $f' = (y \to f(\beta y))$ for some $\beta \in \mathbb{K}^{\times}$ then $\mathfrak{D}(f', I) = \beta \cdot \mathfrak{D}(f, I)$.
\item[(v)] For any $f \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{K}, \mathbb{Q}) - \{0\}$, there is a unique element $\xi \in \mathbb{K}^{\times}$ such that $f = (y \to \operatorname{Tr}(\xi y))$. In particular:
$$\mathfrak{D}(f, I) = (\xi) \cdot I \cdot \mathfrak{d}.$$
\item[(vi)] For a fixed fractional ideal $I$, all different ideals $\mathfrak{D}(f, I)$ belong to the class of $I \times \mathfrak{d}$ in the class group of $\mathbb{K}$.
\item[(vii)] If $f(I) \subset \mathbb{Z}$ then $\mathfrak{D}(f, I) \subset \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$. In addition, if $f(I) = \mathbb{Z}$ then $\mathfrak{D}(f, I)$ is a primitive integral ideal.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: See [\hspace{1sp}\cite{thesis}, Lemma III.12]. The proofs are straightforward and require only elementary facts on fractional ideals.

label: lemmalinktarget
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
First, since $a(L) = \mathbb{Z}$ and $\tilde{a}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}) = \mathbb{Z}$, it follows from lemma \ref{lemmabasicdifferent}, (vii) that these different ideals are primitive integral. Secondly, recall from (\ref{eqlienata}) that 
$$a = \left(y \to \tilde{a}\left(\frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\mathcal{N}(h/m)}{\mathcal{N}(L)}\cdot\frac{m}{h}\cdot y \right) \right).$$
Thus, it follows from lemma \ref{lemmabasicdifferent}, (iv) that
$$\mathfrak{D}(a, L) = \frac{\tilde{\lambda}}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\mathcal{N}(h/m)}{\mathcal{N}(L)}\cdot\frac{m}{h}\cdot \mathfrak{D}(\tilde{a}, L) $$
and using lemma \ref{lemmabasicdifferent}, (iii) we get the desired relation:
$$\lambda \cdot\mathfrak{D}(a, L) = \tilde{\lambda}\cdot \frac{\mathcal{N}(h/m)}{\mathcal{N}(L)}\cdot\frac{m}{h}L\cdot\mathfrak{D}(\tilde{a}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}).$$

label: calculdifferent
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is essentially the same as the proof given in [\hspace{1sp}\cite{cohen}, Proposition 4.8.19]\, for the usual different ideal. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the matrix $(f(e_ie'_j))_{0 \leq i,j \leq r+1}$. Let  us denote by $m_{ij}$ the coefficients of $\mathcal{M}^{-1}$ so that:
$$\sum_{k = 0}^{r+1} f(e_je'_k)m_{kl} = \delta_{jl}$$
where $\delta_{jl}$ is Kronecker's symbol. Let $x = \iota((x_0, \dots, x_{r+1})^{T})$ and $y = \sum_{j = 0}^{r+1} y_j e_j$ where the $x_i$'s are rational numbers and the $y_i$'s are integers. Then:
\begin{align*}
f(xy) & = f\left(\left(\sum_{j = 0}^{r+1} y_je_j\right) \times \left(\sum_{k = 0}^{r+1} e'_k \sum_{l = 0}^{r+1} m_{kl}x_l\right)\right) \\
f(xy) & =\sum_{j = 0}^{r+1} y_j \sum_{l = 0}^{r+1} \left(\sum_{k = 0}^{r+1} f(e_je'_k)  m_{kl}\right) x_l \\
f(xy) & =\sum_{j = 0}^{r+1} y_j x_j
\end{align*}
Therefore, $f(xy) \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $y \in I$ if and only if $x_j \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $0 \leq j \leq r+1$ and $\mathfrak{D}(f, I)^{-1} = \iota(\mathbb{Z}^{r+2})$.

label: lemmaAUM
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmaAUM}
The two following matrix equalities hold:
$$(\mathbf{0}~\mathcal{A}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^{T} \mathcal{M}^{T}, ~~ \text{ and }~~ (\mathbf{0}~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^{T} \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{T} $$
where $^T$ stands for transposition and $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}$ is the matrix defined in (\ref{deftildematu}). As a consequence, $\tilde{\lambda} \mid s$ and $\tilde{\lambda} \mid \tilde{s}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the matrix $(\mathbf{0}~\mathcal{A})$ is given by its coefficients $a(u_j e_l)$ for $0 \leq j \leq r$ and $0 \leq l \leq r+1$. Replacing $u_j$ by its expression $u_j = \sum_{k = 0}^j \tilde{c}_{jk0} \tilde{e}_k$ gives $a(u_j e_l) = \sum_{k = 0}^j \tilde{c}_{jk0}a(\tilde{e}_ke_l)$. Thus:
$$(\mathbf{0}~\mathcal{A}) =  \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0\\ \tilde{c}_{100} & \tilde{c}_{110} & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \tilde{c}_{r00} & \tilde{c}_{r10} & \tilde{c}_{r20} & \dots & \tilde{c}_{rr0} & 0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a(\tilde{e}_0 e_0) &\dots & a(\tilde{e}_0 e_l) & \dots & a(\tilde{e}_0 e_{r+1}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ a(\tilde{e}_j e_0) &\dots & a(\tilde{e}_j e_l) & \dots & a(\tilde{e}_j e_{r+1}) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
a(\tilde{e}_{r+1} e_0) &\dots & a(\tilde{e}_{r+1} e_l) & \dots & a(\tilde{e}_{r+1} e_{r+1}) \\\end{pmatrix}  $$
which is exactly the statement that $(\mathbf{0}~\mathcal{A}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^{T} \mathcal{M}^T$. Let us now analyse this relation more precisely, by introducing two auxiliary square matrices $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0$ and $\mathcal{M}_0$ of size $r+1$ such that
$$\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}} = \begin{pmatrix} & & \\ & \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0 & \\ & & \\ \hline 0 & \dots & 0\end{pmatrix} \text{ and } \mathcal{M} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \dots & 0 & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \pm1 \\ \hline & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \ast \\  & \mathcal{M}_0 & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \vdots \\ & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \ast \end{pmatrix}.$$
Then the relation $(\mathbf{0}~\mathcal{A}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^{T} \mathcal{M}^T$ reduces to $\mathcal{A} = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^{T}\mathcal{M}_0^T$ and taking determinants gives 
$$s = \mathrm{det}(\mathcal{A}) = \mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T) \times \mathrm{det}(\mathcal{M}_0^T) = \tilde{\lambda}.\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{M}_0) \in \tilde{\lambda}. \mathbb{Z}.$$
Thus $\tilde{\lambda} \mid s$. The proof that $(\mathbf{0}~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^T \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^T$ and that $\tilde{\lambda} \mid \tilde{s}$ is essentially the same.

label: defhelper
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defhelper}
An integral ideal $\mathfrak{H}$ is a helper ideal if either $\mathfrak{H} = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ or $\mathfrak{H}$ is a primitive ideal coprime to $q\cdot N\cdot \prod_{\rho}\tilde{t}_{\rho}$ such that $p_{\mathfrak{H}}/\mathfrak{H}$ is a cyclic group of order $p_{\mathfrak{H}}$, where $\mathfrak{H} \cap \mathbb{Z} = p_{\mathfrak{H}}\,\mathbb{Z}$. An extended helper ideal is an ideal of the form $m\cdot\mathfrak{H}$ where $m$ is a positive integer coprime to $q$ and $\mathfrak{H}$ is a helper ideal.
head: environment

label: lemmacebotarevhelper
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmacebotarevhelper}
Any class in the class group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$ contains infinitely many helper ideals of the form $p\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} \cdot \mathfrak{p}^{-1}$ where $p$ is a rational prime and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of norm $p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Fix a class $\mathfrak{C}$ in the class group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$. By Cebotarev's density theorem (see for instance [\hspace{1sp}\cite{Cox}, Theorem 8.17]), there are infinitely many prime ideals of prime norm in the class $\mathfrak{C}^{-1}$, that is to say there are infinitely many pairs $(p, \mathfrak{p})$ where $p$ is a rational prime and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of norm $p$ in $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ such that $\mathfrak{p} \in \mathfrak{C}^{-1}$. For any of these pairs, the integral ideal $p\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} \cdot \mathfrak{p}^{-1}$ is a helper ideal in the class $\mathfrak{C}$ of $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$.
head: environment

label: propexistencebasepoints
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eqdeterlambda
title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first prove that these ideals are generated by an admissible base point for each permutation $\rho$. It follows from the hypothesis (\ref{hypothesisconstantclass}) that the class of the ideal $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}$ in the class group $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$ is independent of $\rho$. Let us then denote by $\mathfrak{C}$ the common class of the fractional ideals $\frac{N}{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}$ in $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$. By lemma \ref{lemmacebotarevhelper} there exists a helper ideal $\mathfrak{H}$ coprime to $q\cdot N \cdot \prod_{\rho} \tilde{t}_{\rho}$ in the class $\mathfrak{C}^{-1}$. This implies that the fractional ideals $\frac{N}{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho} \cdot \mathfrak{H}$ all belong to the trivial class in $\mathrm{Cl}(\mathfrak{f}, \mathbb{Z})$. This means that there are elements $g_{\rho} \in \mathbb{K}$ coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$ and integers $k_{\rho} \in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ such that for each $\rho \in \mathfrak{S}_{n-2}$:
$$\begin{cases} g_{\rho} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} & =\frac{N}{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho} \cdot \mathfrak{H} \\ g_{\rho} & \equiv k_{\rho} \mathrm{~mod~} \mathfrak{f}.\end{cases} $$
For each permutation $\rho$, let us fix a positive integer $m_{\rho}$ satisfying $k_{\rho} m_{\rho} \equiv 1 \mathrm{~mod~} \mathfrak{q}$. Then, the fractional ideals $m_{\rho} \cdot \frac{N}{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho} \cdot \mathfrak{H}$ all belong to the trivial class of the wide class group at $\mathfrak{f}$ as they are generated by the element $m_{\rho} g_{\rho} \equiv 1 \mathrm{~mod~} \mathfrak{f}$. The base point $h_{\rho} = q \cdot m_{\rho} \cdot g_{\rho}$ is thus an admissible base point in the sense of Definition \ref{defadmissible} and it satisfies 
$$h_{\rho}\, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} = \frac{qN}{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}} \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}\cdot m_{\rho}\cdot \mathfrak{H}. $$
Let us now prove that the base points $h_{\rho}$ are compatible. To this end we use lemma \ref{lemmalinktarget} as for each $\rho$:
$$\lambda_{\rho} \cdot\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L) = \tilde{\lambda}_{\rho}\cdot \frac{\mathcal{N}(h_{\rho}/m_{\rho})}{\mathcal{N}(L)}\cdot\frac{m_{\rho}}{h_{\rho}}L\cdot\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}.$$ 
By definition of the base point $h_{\rho}$ we have:
$$\frac{m_{\rho}}{h_{\rho}}L\cdot\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho} = \frac{\mathfrak{f}}{q} \cdot \frac{\mathfrak{a}}{N} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1}$$
and
$$\frac{\mathcal{N}(h_{\rho}/m_{\rho})}{\mathcal{N}(L)} = \frac{q^n}{\mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{f})} \cdot N^{n-1} \cdot \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho})\cdot  p_{\mathfrak{H}}^{n-1}.$$
Putting everything together we obtain:
\begin{equation}\label{eqdeterlambda}\lambda_{\rho} \cdot\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L) = \tilde{\lambda}_{\rho}\cdot \frac{q^{n-1} \mathfrak{f}}{\mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{f})} \cdot N^{n-2} \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}^{n-2} \cdot \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}) \cdot \mathfrak{a} \cdot \frac{p_{\mathfrak{H}}}{\mathfrak{H}}.
\end{equation}
Now, it follows from \ref{lemmabasicdifferent}, (vii) that $\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L)$ is a primitive integral ideal, which means that $\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L) \subset k \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ for some integer $k$ implies that $k = \pm 1$. This means that the largest integer dividing the right-hand side of (\ref{eqdeterlambda}) is precisely $\lambda_{\rho}$. We note that if $Q$ is the largest integer satisfying $\mathfrak{f} \subset Q\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ then:
$$\frac{q^{n-1} \mathfrak{f}}{\mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{f})} = \frac{(q/Q)^{n-1} \mathfrak{f}/Q}{\mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{f}/Q)} $$
and $\mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{f}/Q)$ is a divisor of $(q/Q)^{n-1}$. Now, since the integral ideals $\mathfrak{f}/Q$, $p_{\mathfrak{H}}/\mathfrak{H}$ and $\mathfrak{a}$ are mutually coprime and primitive integral we obtain the desired equalities:
$$\begin{cases} \mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L) & = \frac{\mathfrak{f}}{Q}\cdot \frac{p_{\mathfrak{H}}}{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot\mathfrak{a}, \\ \lambda_{\rho} & = \tilde{\lambda}_{\rho} \cdot\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}_{\rho}) \cdot\frac{Q q^{n-1}}{\mathcal{N}(f)} \cdot N^{n-2} \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}^{n-2}\end{cases}$$
where $p_{\mathfrak{H}} \,\mathbb{Z} = \mathfrak{H} \cap \mathbb{Z}$.
In particular, the generalised different ideal $\mathfrak{D}(a_{\rho}, L)$ is independent of $\rho$ and thus the base points $(h_{\rho})_{\rho}$ are compatible. Lastly, plugging the value we have obtained for $\lambda_{\rho}$ in the fundamental relation (\ref{formulafundam}) gives the equality:
$$\ell_{\rho}\cdot t_{\rho} = \frac{q}{Q} \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \tilde{t}_{\rho}.$$
This completes the proof.

label: talphabasediff
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{talphabasediff}
The matrix $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}$ is integral and satisfies:
$$\tilde{t}\cdot\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} \tilde{x}_0 & \dots & \tilde{x}_r & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \pm \tilde{t} \\ \hline & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\  & \widetilde{\mathcal{B}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^{T} & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \vdots \\ & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix}$$
where $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0$ is the square matrix of size $r+1$ formed by the top $r+1$ rows of $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}$ and $\tilde{x}_0, \dots, \tilde{x}_r$ are integers. As a consequence, the fractional ideal $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}^{-1}$ is integral and it admits the $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $[\tilde{\beta}_0, \dots, \tilde{\beta}_r, \tilde{t}]$ where for any $0 \leq k \leq r$:
$$\tilde{\beta}_k = \tilde{x}_k + \sum_{j = k}^r \tilde{c}_{jk0}\tilde{\alpha}_j.$$
In addition $\tilde{t} \in \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}$ and 
\begin{equation}\label{eqtttn}\tilde{t}^{n-1}  = \tilde{\lambda} \cdot \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}) \cdot |\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathcal{B}})|.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us write $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$ as:
$$\widetilde{\mathcal{M}} = \begin{pmatrix} &\hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & & & \\ X & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & & M & \\ &\hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & & & \\ \hline \rule{0pt}{0.9\normalbaselineskip} Z & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & & Y &\end{pmatrix}$$
where $M$ is a square matrix of size $r+1$. By definition of $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$, the coefficient $Z = \tilde{a}(\tilde{e}_{r+1})$ is $\pm 1$. The matrix $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}$ has a last row filled with zeroes, thus we denote as before by $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0$ the square matrix formed by its top $r+1$ rows. Then, since $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$ is symmetric, we may rewrite the equality $(\mathbf{0}~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}) = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}^{T} \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{T}$ as $\mathbf{0} = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T X$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}} = \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T M$. The matrix $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0$ is invertible when seen as a matrix with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$ as $\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0) = \tilde{\lambda} \neq 0$. Thus we obtain $X = 0$ and 
$$\widetilde{\mathcal{B}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T = \tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathcal{A}}^{-1} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T = \tilde{t} \cdot M^{-1}. $$
Hence $\tilde{t} \cdot M^{-1}$ is an integral matrix and
$$\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1} = \tilde{t} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} & \pm YM^{-1} & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \pm 1 \\ \hline & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\  & M^{-1} & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \vdots \\ & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} \tilde{x}_0 & \dots & \tilde{x}_r & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \pm \tilde{t} \\ \hline & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\  & \widetilde{\mathcal{B}} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^{T} & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & \vdots \\ & & & \hspace*{-\arraycolsep}\vline\hspace*{-\arraycolsep} & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix}$$
for some integers $\tilde{x}_0, \dots, \tilde{x}_r$. As a consequence the matrix $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}$ is integral, and since it represents the fractional ideal $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}^{-1}$ in the basis $\tilde{B}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ this ideal is integral. As a consequence the integral ideal $\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}$ is a divisor of $\tilde{t} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ and $\tilde{t} \in \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}$. In addition, taking determinants gives the equality:
$$\tilde{t}^{n-1} = |\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0)| \cdot |\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathcal{M}})| \cdot |\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathcal{B}})|   = \tilde{\lambda} \cdot \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}) \cdot |\mathrm{det}(\widetilde{\mathcal{B}})|.$$

Let us now denote by $\tilde{\beta}_k$ the element of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ corresponding to the $(k+1)$-th column of $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}$ for $0 \leq k \leq r$. Then by definition of $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}$, the family $[\tilde{\beta}_0, \dots, \tilde{\beta}_r, \tilde{t}]$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}^{-1}$. We now only need to make the link between this family and the family $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r$ explicit. Recall that the columns of the matrix $\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}$ represent the elements $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r$ and that:
$$\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0^T = \begin{pmatrix} \tilde{c}_{000} = 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0\\ \tilde{c}_{100} & \tilde{c}_{110} & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ \tilde{c}_{r00} & \tilde{c}_{r10} & \tilde{c}_{r20} & \dots & \tilde{c}_{rr0} & 0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Therefore, we get $\tilde{\beta}_k = \tilde{x}_k + \sum_{j = k}^r \tilde{c}_{jk0} \tilde{\alpha}_j$ as claimed.
head: environment

label: lemmalmin
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmalmin}
There are integers $m_0, \dots, m_r$ such that $\tilde{\alpha}_0 + m_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r + m_r \in \mathfrak{a} \cdot (p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1})$. As a consequence, the level $\ell$ is divisible by $N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}$. Moreover, if $q'$ is the smallest divisor of $q$ satisfying $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r \in \mathbb{Z} + \mathfrak{f}/q'$ then $\ell$ is divisible by $(q/q') \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}$. In particular, if $I =\mathfrak{f}/Q$ is such that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/I$ is cyclic, $(q/Q) \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}$ divides $\ell$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The groups $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/\mathfrak{a} \simeq \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ and $p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1} \simeq \mathbb{Z}/p_{\mathfrak{H}}\mathbb{Z}$ are cyclic, therefore any of the $\tilde{\alpha}_j$ is congruent to an integer modulo $\mathfrak{a}$ and to an integer modulo $p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1}$. Since $\mathfrak{a}$ and $p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1}$ are coprime by assumption, it follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem that there are integers $m_0, \dots, m_r$ such that $\tilde{\alpha}_0 + m_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r + m_r \in \mathfrak{a} \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1}$. This gives for any $0 \leq j \leq r$, $(\tilde{\alpha}_j + m_j) h \in m \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} L$ and by definition of $\ell$ this implies that $N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \mid \ell$. 

Let us now discuss the  $q$-part of $\ell$. Since $\mathfrak{f} \cap \mathbb{Z} = q\mathbb{Z}$ the fractional ideal $q\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}} \cdot \mathfrak{f}^{-1} = q/\mathfrak{f}$ is integral and therefore its inverse $\mathfrak{f}/q$ contains $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$. Since $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r$ are elements of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}$ we have $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r \in \mathbb{Z} + \mathfrak{f}/q$. Let $J = \{ k \in \mathbb{Z} - \{ 0\} ~|~ \tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r \in \mathbb{Z} + \mathfrak{f}/k\}$. This set is non-empty as $q \in J$. In addition, if $k \in J$ and $k' \in \mathbb{Z} -\{0\}$ then $kk' \in J$ and if $k, k' \in J$, the gcd $(k, k')$ belongs to $J$. Thus $J = q' (\mathbb{Z} - \{0\})$ for a unique positive divisor $q'$ of $q$. Since $\mathfrak{f}/q', \mathfrak{a}, p_{\mathfrak{H}}$ are two-by-two coprime, by the Chinese remainder theorem we get that $\tilde{\alpha}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r \in \mathbb{Z} + (\mathfrak{f}/q') \cdot \mathfrak{a} \cdot (p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \mathfrak{H}^{-1})$. It follows that $\tilde{\alpha}_0h, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_rh \in \mathbb{Z} h + m\cdot (q/q') \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} L$ which implies that $(q/q')\cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \mid \ell$. Lastly, if $I = \mathfrak{f}/Q$ is such that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/I$ is cyclic, then $Q \in J$ and therefore $q'$ divides $Q$. Thus $q/Q$ divides $q/q'$ and $(q/Q) \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \mid \ell$.
head: environment

label: lemmalt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemmalt}
Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/\mathfrak{f}$ is cyclic, that $\tilde{\lambda} = 1$ and that $\tilde{t}$ is coprime to $q$. Then $\ell = q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \tilde{t}$ and $t = s = 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\tilde{\lambda} = 1$, we have $\widetilde{\mathfrak{U}}_0 = I_{r+1}$ and $\tilde{\beta}_k = \tilde{x}_k + \tilde{\alpha}_k$ in lemma \ref{talphabasediff}. Thus, the ideal $\tilde{t} \cdot \widetilde{\mathfrak{D}}^{-1}$ admits the $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $[\tilde{\alpha}_0+\tilde{x}_0, \dots, \tilde{\alpha}_r + \tilde{x}_r, \tilde{t}\,]$. It then follows that 
$$(\tilde{\alpha}_j + \tilde{x}_j)h \in m \tilde{t} L $$
and therefore by definition of $\ell$ we get $\tilde{t} \mid \ell$. From lemma \ref{lemmalmin} we also have $q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \mid \ell$ as $Q= 1$ when $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/\mathfrak{f}$ is cyclic. By assumption, $\tilde{t}$ is coprime to $q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}}$, therefore $q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \tilde{t} \mid \ell$. Since $ \ell t = q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \tilde{t}$ we conclude that 
$$\begin{cases} \ell & = q \cdot N \cdot p_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot \tilde{t} \\ t & = 1.\end{cases}$$
Lastly, $s$ and $t$ share the same prime factors, therefore $s = 1$.
